name: Min Dong Chinese
sweep_summary: Min Dong (Fuzhou) is not in the catalog. Three title-hits: (1) Chan 1985 UW dissertation 'Fuzhou Phonology: A Non-Linear Analysis of Tone and Stress' -- directly about Fuzhou stress, but only available via ProQuest/UMI (author's OSU page confirms; no open copy anywhere probed); high acquisition priority, together with her 1984 UWWPL article 'Stress and vowel quality changes in the Fuzhou dialect' (8: 19-38). (2) Zhao & Bao 2024 review of You 2020 (Routledge prosodic-phonology monograph on Fuzhou sandhi domains) -- paywalled, one-line abstract; low priority (the book itself would be medium). (3) Chen 2019, Language and Linguistics 20(1), CC BY -- fetched sources and read; pp. 62-64 state that Fuzhou prosodic words end in a right-headed disyllabic foot, the final syllable being the strongest (retains citation tone/vowel/weight) and all non-final syllables weak, citing Wright 1983 duration data and M. Chan 1985 / Jiang-King / L. Chan 1998. Best statement read: Chen 2019 p. 64 (fixed final prominence, tone-sandhi-diagnosed); no catalog source to supersede. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, WorldCat, HathiTrust, UMass ScholarWorks and UBC cIRcle were rate-limited or blocked, so Wright 1983 and Jiang-King 1996 (both potentially open dissertations) were not retrieved.

new_statements.quote: Each PrWd contains only one disyllabic right-headed foot. The foot is the head of the PrWd, and it stands on the right edge of the PrWd. [...] First, the final syllable is the head of the disyllabic foot, and the foot is the head of the PrWd. Therefore, the final syllable is the strongest syllable in each PrWd. The non-final syllable(s) are either the non-headed syllable of the foot, or the unfooted syllable(s) in the PrWd. In both cases, the non-final syllables are relatively weak in the PrWd domain. The strong status ensures feature stability while the weak status leads to feature changes.
new_statements.citation: Chen, Aishu (2019). Interactions between prosody and morphosyntax in Fuzhou VO phrases. Language and Linguistics 20(1): 46-84.
new_statements.locator: pp. 62 (ex. 13 and following paragraph) and 64 (ex. 15 and following paragraph)
new_statements.reading: Fuzhou (Min Dong) word-level prominence is fixed on the final syllable of the prosodic word / tone-sandhi domain: a right-headed disyllabic foot at the right edge, with all preceding syllables weak. Evidence is metrical-phonological (final syllable keeps citation tone, vowel quality and weight; non-final syllables undergo sandhi and weight reduction) plus Wright's (1983) duration measurements; the author attributes the right-headed-foot analysis to Wright 1983, M. Chan 1985, Jiang-King 1995-1999 and L. Chan 1998. It is an analytic statement in a tone language, not a field description of audible stress, so a catalog coding would be 'final / right-edge prominence (metrical, tone-sandhi-diagnosed)'. Chan 1985 (ProQuest-only) is the primary source and would be the better citation if acquired.

sources.citation: Chen, Aishu (2019). Interactions between prosody and morphosyntax in Fuzhou VO phrases. Language and Linguistics 20(1): 46-84. CC BY 4.0.
sources.quote: p. 62: "the disyllabic right-headed foot shown in (13) has also been argued in previous studies based on the evidences from acoustic experiments, and the tone sandhi and vowel alternation patterns observed within a disyllabic word. (13) Fuzhou right-headed foot structure (Wright 1983; M. Chan 1985; Jiang-King 1995, 1996, 1999; L. Chan 1998, among others) Ft / σw σs ... The initial syllable is relatively weak, so it reduces more duration. The final syllable is relatively strong, so it reduces less duration." p. 64: "the final syllable is the head of the disyllabic foot, and the foot is the head of the PrWd. Therefore, the final syllable is the strongest syllable in each PrWd."
sources.note: Fuzhou prosodic words (= tone-sandhi domains, 2-4 syllables) end in a single disyllabic right-headed foot at the right edge; the final syllable is the strongest (retains citation tone, vowel and weight), all non-final syllables are weak (undergo tone sandhi, weight reduction, tone loss for antepenults). Prominence is diagnosed by duration (Wright 1983: initial syllable of a disyllable loses ~2/3 of citation duration, final syllable < 1/3) and by tone/vowel stability, not by a descriptive stress-placement statement; fn. 13 notes duration is the main stress cue in Chinese. I.e. fixed word-final…

sources.note: Landing page gives only a one-line abstract; full text is paywalled (purchase 15 GBP). The reviewed book (You, Shuxiang 2020, Routledge Studies in Chinese Linguistics, 262 pp.; TOC read at routledge.com: introduction; syllable and foot; prosodic word; enclitics and Type A clitic group; phonological phrase; proclitics and Type B clitic group; intonational phrase) is about prosodic domains for tone-sandhi rule application; the 'syllable and foot' chapter would be where foot headedness/stress is stated, but neither the book blurb nor the review page mentions stress.

Chan 1985' among the studies that established the Fuzhou disyllabic right-headed foot (weak initial syllable, strong final syllable) from tone-sandhi and vowel-alternation evidence.
